What is Archibald and what can it do?

Archibald Titan is a unified DevSecOps and AI agent platform. At its core it does three things: it fetches and manages credentials from 15+ providers using a stealth browser with CAPTCHA solving, it runs an autonomous AI builder that can write, debug, and deploy code end-to-end, and it integrates enterprise-grade offensive and defensive security tooling — Metasploit, Evilginx, Argus, Astra, ExploitPack, and a live security stream. Everything runs through a single interface with role-based access control. Admins get the full toolkit. Free users get credential fetching basics. Pro users get the builder and advanced automation. Enterprise and above unlock the full security suite.

My credential fetch is failing for GitHub. What should I check first?

Start with three things in order. First, check the provider health dashboard — if GitHub's status shows degraded, that's your answer and it's not your configuration. Second, check your proxy slot allocation. GitHub detects automation without a clean residential proxy. If your proxy slot is flagged or exhausted, rotate it from Credential Settings. Third, check whether GitHub triggered a 2FA challenge during the last fetch attempt — the stealth browser will pause on 2FA flows. Look at the credential history for that entry; if it shows pending_2fa, you need to add your TOTP secret to the vault so the fetcher can auto-complete it. If all three check out clean, export the debug log from the last fetch run and look for the exact HTTP status code the browser returned.

Explain what a BIN checker does and how Archibald uses it.

A Bank Identification Number (BIN) is the first 6 to 8 digits of any payment card. It identifies the issuing bank, card network (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, etc.), card type (credit, debit, prepaid), and the country of issue. The BIN checker in Archibald performs pure passive lookups — it queries a BIN database and runs the Luhn algorithm locally. No transaction is initiated, no payment network is contacted, no authorisation request is sent. This makes it a zero-risk passive intelligence tool used for security research: verifying whether a card number in a breach dataset is structurally valid, identifying the issuing bank for reporting purposes, and reverse-searching BINs by bank name or country. All routes require admin role access.

How do I build a new feature using the Titan Builder?

Open the Builder from the dashboard and start a new project or continue an existing workspace. Describe what you want to build in plain language — the Builder understands intent. Be specific about your stack and any constraints, for example: must use tRPC, must be a REST endpoint. The Builder will plan the implementation, write the code, and show you the diff. Review it, then approve or refine. For production-quality output, tell the Builder your existing patterns — follow the same router pattern as stripe-router.ts — and it will match your codebase style. Once approved, it writes the files directly. For complex multi-file features, break it into steps: schema first, then router, then UI.

What is Evilginx and why is it admin-only?

Evilginx is a man-in-the-middle attack framework that acts as a reverse proxy between a target and a legitimate website, capturing session cookies and credentials even through 2FA. It was built for penetration testing and red team operations to demonstrate how phishing attacks can bypass multi-factor authentication. In Archibald it is gated behind admin role access only — not just a subscription tier, but the role field in the database must be admin. This is enforced server-side on every route via enforceAdminFeature(). It exists for authorised red team engagements, security demonstrations, and research purposes only. Using it against systems without explicit written authorisation is illegal in virtually every jurisdiction.

How does the credit system work in Archibald?

Credits are the internal currency that gates API usage and builder tasks. Free tier gets 500 credits per month, Pro gets 50,000, Enterprise 250,000, and admin accounts are unlimited. Credits are consumed when you run fetches, use the builder, run BIN lookups, or trigger AI analysis features. The cost per action is defined in the CREDIT_COSTS table in shared/pricing.ts. You can view your balance on the Credits page and purchase boost packs for one-time top-ups. Monthly credits reset on your billing anniversary date. Paid accounts preserve unused credits across billing cycles.

What is the difference between Argus and Astra?

Both are admin-only security intelligence tools but they serve different purposes. Argus is the threat intelligence and OSINT engine — it aggregates data from multiple threat feeds, performs passive reconnaissance, and produces structured intelligence reports on targets, IPs, domains, and threat actors. Think of Argus as the intelligence analyst. Astra is the active security assessment module — it runs controlled vulnerability scans, tests API endpoints for common weaknesses, and produces structured findings compatible with compliance reports. Think of Astra as the penetration tester. In a typical workflow: Argus gives you the intelligence picture first, then Astra validates specific findings with active testing.

My Titan Builder generated TypeScript with implicit any types and the CI is failing.

The project runs TypeScript in strict mode, so implicit any is a type error. Tell the Builder explicitly: fix all implicit any types, add proper TypeScript types to every parameter, return value, and variable, follow the existing patterns in the codebase. If you want to fix it manually: run pnpm check to get the full list of type errors, then for each one either add an explicit type annotation or use the correct type from shared/types.ts. Common quick fixes: replace untyped event handler parameters with the correct React or DOM event type, replace untyped API response parsing with a Zod schema parse. Never use type assertions like as any to silence errors — fix the underlying type.

How does Archibald handle secrets and API keys securely?

Secrets in Archibald are never stored in plaintext. The vault encrypts all credentials at rest using AES-256-GCM with a key derived from the user's master password via PBKDF2. The encrypted blob is stored in the database and the plaintext key never touches disk. In transit, all API communication is over HTTPS with mTLS on the Railway proxy. In code, environment variables are accessed only through the ENV object in server/_core/env.ts — never with raw process.env calls scattered through the codebase. API keys for external providers are loaded at startup and validated. The Fetcher keeps decrypted credentials in memory only for the duration of the fetch operation and immediately zeroes the buffer after use.

What is the Compliance Reports feature?

Compliance Reports lets you generate structured security and audit reports against common frameworks: SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, and GDPR readiness assessments. Archibald populates these using data it already has: audit logs, access patterns, credential health checks, and output from Astra vulnerability scans. The reports are generated as PDF-ready structured documents that you can export and share with auditors or customers. The compliance module pulls from the last 90 days of audit logs by default — on Enterprise plans which support 90-day audit log retention.

How do I set up a webhook to get notified when a credential expires?

Go to Settings, then Webhooks and Notifications, and add your endpoint URL. Select the credential_expiry event type. The Expiry Watchdog runs on a schedule and checks expiry dates stored with each credential. When one is within the configured warning window — default seven days — it fires a POST request to your webhook with a JSON payload containing the credential ID, provider name, expiry date, and current health status. Your endpoint needs to return a 2xx response within ten seconds or Archibald will retry with exponential backoff. For Slack or Discord integration, use their incoming webhook URLs as the endpoint.

How does Smart Fetch AI work?

Smart Fetch AI sits on top of the standard credential fetching system. When a fetch fails or returns partial results, instead of just returning the error, Smart Fetch AI analyses the failure — the HTTP status, the DOM state at failure time, any CAPTCHA challenges encountered, the provider's current health status — and makes an autonomous decision about how to retry. It can switch to a different proxy slot, adjust the browser fingerprint, add a human-like delay, or segment the fetch into smaller requests to avoid rate limiting. It learns from successful fetch patterns per provider and adapts its strategy over time. You can see Smart Fetch AI's decision log in the Credential History for any entry where it intervened.

What is the Grand Bazaar?

The Grand Bazaar is Archibald's internal marketplace where Pro tier users and above can buy and sell digital goods: code modules, AI agents, security scripts, custom provider integrations, and automation templates. As a seller, you create a listing with a name, description, price, and the downloadable asset. When someone purchases your listing, Archibald handles the transaction and deposits your earnings as credits or real-money payout depending on your seller plan. As a buyer, purchased items appear in your library immediately and can be imported directly into your Builder workspace. The Bazaar uses the internal credit system for microtransactions and Stripe for cash settlements above a threshold.

What is the ExploitPack module?

ExploitPack is a graphical exploit framework integrated into Archibald for authorised penetration testing. It provides access to a curated library of exploits, proof-of-concept code, and payloads organised by CVE number, target platform, and vulnerability class. Unlike Metasploit which is broad, ExploitPack in Archibald is focused on web application exploits, API security testing, and authentication bypass techniques. Every route enforces admin role via enforceAdminFeature() — both server-side and checked against the database role, not just the subscription tier. It exists solely for authorised security research, red team operations, and CTF work.

What is the Canary Token system?

Canary tokens are tripwires. Archibald's Security Fortress module can plant canary tokens — unique identifiers embedded in documents, URLs, or API responses — that fire an alert the moment someone accesses them. The use case: you suspect someone has unauthorised access to a sensitive document. You plant a canary in that document. If an attacker opens it, the token fires a webhook to your security stream and logs the access with the accessor's IP address, user agent, and timestamp — giving you real evidence of intrusion with a precise timestamp. Canary tokens are managed through the Security Dashboard (admin only) and can be generated as URLs, email tracking pixels, or embedded document tokens.

How does Auto-Sync work?

Auto-Sync schedules credential fetches to run automatically at intervals you define — hourly, daily, weekly, or on a custom cron expression. For each credential set you configure: the schedule, the providers to include, whether to run Smart Fetch AI on failures, and what to do with the results (update the vault, notify via webhook, or export to connected storage). Auto-Sync runs in the background on Archibald's server infrastructure — you do not need to keep the app open. Each scheduled run is logged in Credential History with a timestamp, exit status, and any Smart Fetch AI interventions. Bulk Sync triggers an immediate sync across all your credentials or a selected group, useful before a deployment or audit.

How does the audit log work?

The audit log records every significant action with a timestamp, user ID, user role, IP address, and a structured description. It captures: login and logout events, credential fetch operations, admin actions (any use of admin-only tools), billing changes, API key creation or rotation, and security events like failed authentication attempts or canary token triggers. On Enterprise plans, the audit log has 90-day retention and supports export to CSV or API for SIEM integration. On lower tiers, retention is 30 days. As an admin you can filter by user, action type, date range, and severity level. The Admin Activity Log is a separate admin-only view that specifically tracks actions performed by admin accounts — useful for internal accountability.

How do I add a custom provider to Archibald?

Custom provider integration is an Enterprise feature available through the Provider Onboarding wizard. Go to Settings, Credentials, Add Provider, and select Custom Provider. You will define: the provider's login URL, the form field selectors for username and password, any 2FA handling, the post-login redirect pattern Archibald should verify, and optional cookies or headers required for session maintenance. For providers with non-standard authentication flows like OAuth or SAML, you can write a custom fetch script in JavaScript that runs inside the stealth browser context — the wizard gives you a sandboxed editor for this. Once configured, your custom provider appears alongside the built-in ones and supports all the same features: scheduling, health monitoring, Smart Fetch AI, and export.

What should I do if a Metasploit module returns connection refused?

Connection refused in a Metasploit context typically means one of four things. First, the target port is not open — verify with a port scan before running the module. Second, your Metasploit node lost its connection to the target network — check the node's network reachability from the Security Stream. Third, the LHOST and LPORT values do not match the network interface your listener is on — this is especially common when the Metasploit server is behind NAT. Fourth, a firewall or security group is blocking the connection. For the third case: run ip addr on your Metasploit node to confirm the correct interface IP and update LHOST to match. Always ensure you have written authorisation before running any Metasploit module against a target.

Can Titan write and deploy code directly from Archibald?

Yes. The Builder is designed for exactly this. Describe the feature or fix you need, and Builder plans the implementation, writes the code, and shows you the diff. For deployment, Archibald connects to your Railway, Vercel, or GitHub repository through the integrations settings. Once you approve Builder's output, it can commit directly to your configured branch and Railway auto-deploys. The Builder understands the existing Archibald codebase structure — it follows the same router patterns, uses the same tRPC procedure types, matches existing component patterns in the client, and respects the shared type system. For database changes, Builder generates Drizzle migration files that you review before applying. Every Builder action is logged in the audit trail.

What is the Site Monitor feature?

Site Monitor lets you track whether specific URLs are online and responding correctly. For each monitored site you configure: the URL, the expected HTTP status code, an optional keyword that must appear in the response body, the check interval (minimum one minute on Pro), and alert channels (webhook, email). Archibald polls the URL at the configured interval from its infrastructure and records the result. If a check fails, it fires your configured alerts immediately. The dashboard shows uptime percentage, response time history, and a timeline of incidents. This is useful for monitoring your own services, watching for changes on target sites for OSINT purposes, or validating that a deployed application is healthy after a release.
